opus-5.5.text:
I think what I valued most was the freedom. The Fundamental Science Program at Tsinghua gave students a strong foundation in both math and physics, but it didn't force you to commit to one narrow direction too early. You took a lot of rigorous core courses, and then you had a lot of room to follow whatever you found interesting.

For me, that meant I could try different things. I could take more advanced math courses, I could go deeper into theoretical physics, and I could talk to professors in different areas to see what research actually looked like. Nobody said, "You're in this track, so you have to do this." The attitude was more like: if you're curious about something and willing to work hard on it, go ahead.

I think that matters a lot when you're young, because at eighteen or nineteen you don't really know what you're good at or what you'll love. If the system locks you in too early, you might end up optimizing for the wrong thing. The program trusted students to explore, and it surrounded you with very strong peers who were also exploring. So you learned a lot just from seeing what other people were excited about.

Looking back, that habit of following my own curiosity, and being comfortable switching directions when something more interesting came up, has stayed with me. It helped later when I moved from physics into AI. That kind of change felt less scary because I had always been encouraged to learn new things from the fundamentals rather than stick to one fixed path.

r001.rationale: The response says students had room to follow their interests and specifically mentions taking advanced math courses alongside theoretical physics, showing that the program allowed academic exploration outside physics.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing I valued most was that it didn't try to decide for you. When I entered Tsinghua, I honestly wasn't sure what I wanted to do. I liked physics, I liked math, I was curious about computer science, but I couldn't tell you which one I'd commit my life to. A normal department would have put me on a track immediately, and the track decides a lot of things before you've had a chance to find out who you are.

The Fundamental Science Program basically said: take a year or two, learn the real foundations across physics and math, and figure it out. That sounds simple, but it's actually rare. Most systems optimize for efficiency, for getting you to a specialty quickly. This one optimized for the student's own curiosity, and it trusted that if you gave serious people real freedom and a strong base, they'd find something worth doing.

The other thing is that it took interest seriously as a signal, not as a luxury. There was a culture where if you were genuinely fascinated by something, that was considered a legitimate reason to pursue it, even if it wasn't the obvious career move. I think that mattered for me later. A lot of what I ended up doing in AI, the reasoning and agents work, came from following questions I found interesting rather than questions that were fashionable at the time. The program gave me the habit of trusting that instinct, and also the breadth to be able to act on it when the instinct pointed somewhere unexpected.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the program gave students time and freedom to explore, describing foundations in both physics and math and treating genuine fascination as a legitimate reason to pursue a subject.

astra-6.text: What I valued most was the freedom to explore. You didn’t have to arrive knowing exactly what you wanted to study and then stay on that path. There was room to develop a broad foundation, discover what genuinely interested you, and change direction as you learned more. I think that respect for students’ curiosity is really important.

r001.rationale: The response describes freedom to explore, build a broad foundation, and change direction, but does not state that students could pursue interests outside physics.
